jobs.desc: Backend at a fully digital insurtech. Building and evolving the insurance core and the services behind the full policy lifecycle: Java + Spring Boot microservices with PostgreSQL on Kubernetes. TDD, code review and AI-assisted development with Claude. Observability with Grafana, OpenTelemetry and Sentry.

Worked at the intersection of software engineering and AI. Built the knowledge layer that lets AI understand a team's architecture and conventions — agent design, prompt engineering, context management.
Backend microservice features for job integration flows, with unit tests on every feature delivered. Cloud migration, technical debt reduction, monitoring with Grafana and Datadog on Kubernetes.
Backend microservices with Java 8–17 and Spring Boot, plus frontend features in Angular. Flyway migrations on PostgreSQL and Oracle. Agile delivery with CI/CD. Internal Women in Tech bootcamp.

paragraphs: Deep down, I’ve always been a <mark class="y">fan of languages</mark> and of all the different ways we humans communicate. Technology drew me in too, and one way or another I kept trying to get closer to it, but I was scared enough to shake something that’s already hard: making decisions before you’re even 18.

My first job was at an electronics shop and I was happy there (except when customers weren’t so nice, of course). I loved being surrounded by gadgets and helping people set up their new phones, even if it wasn’t part of my job. I’d look at those Android menus and think, “I’d love to know how to build this”, but it felt so far away… Then I spent six years in logistics, because I had to make a living. It wasn’t for me: I could have stayed in that sector forever, but at what cost?

Today I work as a <mark class="p">Backend Developer</mark> at a fully digital insurtech, with really lovely people. Ten years ago I didn’t see it coming, and maybe not even in 2022, when I left everything behind for a Java bootcamp in a pretty tough transition. In my years in tech I’ve been a fullstack dev, a proxy product owner and a bit of a jack of all trades, and I’m sure this world is where I belong: I’ve learned a lot and keep learning every day, both in and out of working hours.

AI burst in like a bull in a china shop while I was busy surviving between work and my higher vocational degree in Multiplatform Application Development. Things are changing faster and faster, at a dizzying pace. My humanities self and my tech self have always gone hand in hand one way or another, and now they may be <mark class="v">more intertwined than ever</mark>.

I know what it’s like to start from scratch and feel lost, and it has made me more patient with others and with myself. That’s why I try to share what I learn and discover along the way: to make the time I put into it count, to stand up to impostor syndrome every day and, above all, to support and empower other women in tech, whether through the Step4ward community, my ramblings on Twitter, more useful stuff on Medium or the talk I gave at T3chFest in 2024.

tablet.desc: Turns the old tablet in the drawer into an always-on family panel: meals, agenda, tasks, shopping list and weather. Works on 2014 browsers, runs inside Home Assistant OS, and the family edits the lists from Telegram.

sabrosapp.desc: DAM final degree project. Multiplatform restaurant management app: iOS, Android and web.

cacalogo.desc: Personal Android digestive diary app. The official Bristol Stool Scale with a sense of humour, statistics, automatic diagnostics, and two report export modes: medical and friends-edition. Local-first: no tracking, no server data.

diatessaron.desc: Website for my choir, which keeps me going in my free time: concerts, past programmes, gallery and contact form. A static site built with Astro and Tailwind.

nlp.desc: A practice repo to learn some computational linguistics: a script that analyses parts of speech, morphology and named entities with spaCy, plus a small FastAPI API.

closet.desc: App to organise your digital wardrobe. A personal Flutter project I never finished in time, and now there are 234234 just like it. I hope to finish it someday, even if it’s just for me.

kata.desc: TDD kata in Java. Mars Rover problem implemented with clean architecture, JUnit 5, Maven and JaCoCo coverage.

bodas.desc: Two simple countdown sites for two friends’ weddings. The weddings have happened, but I keep them as a memento 💍

talk.talkDesc: Philology and programming are more alike than you think. A journey between human languages and machine languages, exploring how learning languages and learning to code share the same cognitive foundations.
